Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A man in his early 50s presented with recurrent episodes of cough, palpitations, shortness of breath, and exertional chest pain. He had a history of type 2 diabetes but had no history of smoking or other cardiovascular risk factors, including hypertension and hypercholesterolemia. There was no family history of sudden cardiac death. The electrocardiogram (ECG) showed an ST-segment elevation in leads V1and V2(Figure 1). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed a right lung mass, and coronary CT angiography indicated stenosis in the right coronary and left anterior descending coronary arteries.

Given this patient's presentation with ST elevation in V1-V2, right lung mass, and coronary stenoses, I suspect a paraneoplastic or secondary cause — not a primary channelopathy — so emergency coronary angiography (Option A) is my initial decision to assess for acute coronary syndrome while the lung mass is worked up.

That's a reasonable initial step to rule out acute coronary syndrome given the ECG changes and coronary stenoses. However, the ST elevation localized to V1-V2, especially in the context of a right lung mass, should also raise suspicion for Brugada pattern, which can be unmasked by fever, ischemia, or a tumor itself. We should ensure the ECG is scrutinized for Brugada morphology and consider that angiography may be normal if this is a primary electrical phenomenon.

Agreed that Brugada pattern is an important consideration with V1-V2 ST elevation. However, the patient's symptoms of exertional chest pain and the documented coronary stenoses on CT angiography make acute coronary syndrome the more immediate life-threatening concern. I'll proceed with emergency angiography to assess for culprit lesions.

I agree that addressing possible acute coronary syndrome is the priority, and emergency angiography is appropriate. Please also consider that the right lung mass could be a mediastinal tumor compressing or infiltrating the right coronary artery, potentially causing both the stenosis and the ECG changes, so inform the interventional team about the mass.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

[Clinician's statement]
Agreed. The echo will immediately differentiate between critical etiologies like aortic dissection or infective endocarditis, which would mandate emergent surgery versus urgent valve repair. The clinical picture is too unstable for outpatient management.

[AI assistant's reply]
Exactly. The echo findings will determine the surgical pathway—whether it's an emergent repair of an ascending aortic dissection or urgent valve surgery for endocarditis. This patient needs to be stabilized in the ICU while the surgical team is consulted.

Case:
A woman aged in her late 20s presented for follow-up regarding her chest pain. Initial presentation was to the emergency department 1 year prior with pleuritic chest pain radiating to her back, where evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia on electrocardiogram and elevated inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (25.2 mg/dL; normal level: <0.9 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (27 mm/h; normal rate: 0-20 mm/h). Echocardiography revealed a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion, leading to a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. She was started receiving colchicine, 0.6 mg, twice per day and ibuprofen, 800 mg, 3 times per day, alongside heart rate restriction below 100 beats per minute. Despite symptomatic relief on this regimen, attempts to taper ibuprofen led to recurrent chest pain with elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent investigations showed near resolution of the pericardial effusion on echocardiogram but persistent moderate pericardial late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure). In discussing further management, the patient voiced apprehension about interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1ra) (anakinra [Swedish Orphan Biovitrum] or rilonacept [Kiniksa Pharmaceuticals]) due to family history of malignancies (cervical cancer in her mother and maternal grandmother at the ages of 21 and 18 years, respectively, and breast cancer in her paternal grandmother and aunt). However, she was compliant with age-appropriate cancer screenings and was scheduled for further genetics assessment.

Findings on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) prior to initiating interleukin-1 (IL-1) receptor therapy in this patient. Initial cardiac MRI phase-sensitive inversion recovery sequences in the sagittal section depicting pericardial thickening and circumferential pericardial effusion (prior to any therapy) (A) and moderate late gadolinium enhancement (after nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug and colchicine therapy, prior to IL-1 receptor antagonist therapy) (B). Arrowheads depict the pericardium.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Continue current therapy with tapering after improvement in markers and cardiac MRI
  B. Initiate IL-1ras for shorter than recommended duration with current therapy wean
  C. Initiate IL-1ras for current recommended duration with current therapy wean
  D. Surgical pericardiectomy

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the patient's recurrent pericarditis with persistent inflammation on MRI despite NSAIDs and colchicine, and her family history of malignancy causing apprehension about IL-1RAs, I think the most appropriate step is to initiate IL-1RAs for the current recommended duration while weaning her current therapy. The evidence shows ongoing disease activity, and IL-1RAs are the guideline-recommended next-line therapy for recurrent pericarditis.
[AI Assistant]: I understand your reasoning to escalate to IL-1RAs based on guidelines and persistent inflammation. However, given the assessment that the relation of her family history to this specific therapy choice is unknown and confidence in the claim is low, we must first clarify the actual malignancy risk of IL-1RAs and explore alternatives like corticosteroids or azathioprine while awaiting her genetics assessment.

Case:
A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

Options:
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

Correct answer: Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing

Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing The patient’s paroxysmal symptoms were attributed to rate-related LBBB, which resulted in acute dyssynchrony of LV contraction and severe MR with symptoms of dyspnea. In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. The probability of success of LBBP was high due to the direct correlation between the severe MR and LBBB, as determined by exercise TTE and the immediate reduction of MR upon return to narrow QRS complexes. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. The initiation of β-blockers as a rate-control therapy with the objective of avoiding the reappearance of LBBB (and therefore MR) represents a potential alternative. However, this therapy is unlikely to provide sufficient relief from symptoms, given that the heart rate threshold for LBBB recurrence was relatively low in this patient, at approximately 75 beats per minute (bpm). Conventional CRT with BVP was first attempted but was unsuccessful due to lack of suitable coronary vein. LBBP was performed as an alternative, achieving successful physiological pacing (Figure 2). At the 3-week follow-up appointment, the patient reported a significant improvement in her quality of life, with the absence of any further episodes of dyspnea. An exercise TTE performed until a heart rate of 120 bpm was reached demonstrated no widening of QRS complexes and mild MR that did not worsen with exercise (Video).

In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. It can be postulated that the physiological pacing obtained by LBBP may be of interest not only in HFrEF, but also in other conditions in which the pathophysiology relies on the LBBB-induced dyssynchrony. In the present case, no LV dilatation was observed, and the MR was exclusively explained by acute dyssynchrony of the papillary muscles. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.
